- Returns a snapshot of the visibility state. While occluded, this window pauses update and draw until it becomes visible again; a closed window returns `false`.
- On macOS, this includes minimized windows, fully covered windows, and windows on another Space. On Windows, it includes minimization or DXGI-reported occlusion. On Linux X11, it includes minimization or full obscuration reported by X11; full-coverage detection applies without a compositing manager.
- For main-thread requirements, see `Window::setApp`.

## Window::setClearColor

- Copies `c` and uses it to clear this window before its draw event and App drawing. Color components are 0–1 floats; the default is `Color(0.05f, 0.05f, 0.08f, 1.0f)`.
- Setting the color does not immediately clear or redraw the window.
- For main-thread requirements, see `Window::setApp`.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    if (auto window = getWindow()) window->setClearColor(Color(0.1f, 0.2f, 0.3f, 1.0f));
}
```

## Window::setSize

- `width` and `height` specify the content area in logical points, excluding window decorations. These units match `Window::getWidth()`, `Window::getHeight()`, and this window's input coordinates.
- Secondary windows use logical coordinates even when pixelPerfect mode is enabled. DPI scaling is handled when converting the requested size to native dimensions.
- Does nothing after the native window closes. For main-thread requirements, see `Window::setApp`.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    if (auto window = getWindow()) window->setSize(800, 600);
}
```

## Window::setFps

- `fps` is the target number of update and draw pairs per second. The default is `0`; values at or below zero run without additional throttling, paced by the display refresh rate.
- A positive target below the display refresh rate skips display ticks to run update and draw at approximately the requested rate. Targets at or above the display refresh rate effectively run on every tick. Linux X11 uses timer pacing based on the measured refresh rate.
- Skipped ticks return before frame work and do not advance this window's update or draw counts. Update and draw share one rate; independent rates and event-driven `redraw()` are main-window features.
- `getFps()` returns this target. For a measured rate, call `getFrameRate()` from this window's update or draw callback.
- For main-thread requirements, see `Window::setApp`.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    if (auto window = getWindow()) window->setFps(30.0f);
}
```

## Window::getFps

- Returns the stored float target, initially `0`, rather than a measured rate. Zero or negative values mean no additional throttling beyond display pacing.
- For target-rate behavior and measurement, see `Window::setFps`; for main-thread requirements, see `Window::setApp`.

## Window::setFullscreen

- Pass `true` to enter fullscreen or `false` to leave it. Does nothing after the native window closes.
- macOS uses native fullscreen with an asynchronous animation. Windows uses a borderless window covering its monitor and restores the saved window style and rectangle on exit. Linux X11 sends an EWMH `_NET_WM_STATE_FULLSCREEN` request to the window manager.
- Size changes are handled through the window's normal resize processing. See `Window::isFullscreen` for platform differences in the reported state.
- For main-thread requirements, see `Window::setApp`.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    if (auto window = getWindow()) window->setFullscreen(true);
}
```

## Window::isFullscreen

- On macOS, reads the native window's current fullscreen state. Transitions are asynchronous and animated, so a request may not be reflected immediately; a closed window returns `false`.
- On Windows and Linux X11, returns the stored fullscreen request flag rather than querying the operating system. Closing the window does not reset this flag, so it can remain `true` after closure.
- For main-thread requirements, see `Window::setApp`.

## Window::toggleFullscreen

- Calls `setFullscreen(!isFullscreen())`. See `Window::setFullscreen` and `Window::isFullscreen` for platform behavior and asynchronous transitions.
- Does nothing after the native window closes. For main-thread requirements, see `Window::setApp`.

## createWindow

- Accepts an optional `WindowSettings` and returns a `shared_ptr<Window>` on success. Attach content with `Window::setApp`.
- Reads `width`, `height`, `title`, `decorated`, `highDpi`, and `sampleCount`. With no argument, these default to 1280 × 720 logical pixels, `"TrussC App"`, decorations enabled, high DPI enabled, and 4× MSAA.
- Other `WindowSettings` fields are not applied, including `fullscreen`, `pixelPerfect`, and `swapInterval`. To enter fullscreen after creation, use `Window::setFullscreen`.
- Supports macOS, Windows, and desktop Linux with X11 and OpenGL. On Web, iOS, Android, and GLES3 Linux builds, logs an error and returns `nullptr`.
- Also logs an error and returns `nullptr` in headless mode or when native window creation fails.
- On desktop Linux, the MSAA sample count comes from the shared configuration negotiated at startup; this call's `sampleCount` does not change it.
- For ownership, main-thread requirements, frame timing, and behavior when closing, see `Window`.

```cpp
// tcApp.h (inside class tcApp : public App)
shared_ptr<Window> secondWindow;
// tcApp.cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    secondWindow = createWindow(WindowSettings().setSize(640, 480).setTitle("Second window"));
    if (secondWindow) secondWindow->setApp(make_shared<App>());
}
```

## WindowSettings

- Pass a `WindowSettings` value to `runApp<AppClass>()`. Its setters return the same settings object for chaining; the default size is 1280 × 720 and the title is `"TrussC App"`.
- `highDpi` defaults to `true`, and `pixelPerfect` defaults to `false`. Normally sizes and drawing coordinates use logical pixels; pixel-perfect mode treats the requested size as framebuffer pixels and uses framebuffer-sized drawing coordinates.
- `sampleCount` requests MSAA and defaults to `4`. `fullscreen` defaults to `false`, and `decorated` defaults to `true`; disabling decorations requests a borderless window on desktop platforms.
- `swapInterval` defaults to `1` for display synchronization; `0` disables it. Use `setSwapInterval()` to configure presentation separately from the update and draw rates.
- `clipboardSize` defaults to 65536 bytes. `setClipboardSize()` sets the backend's text buffer limit; oversized clipboard text can be truncated or rejected depending on the platform.
- `uniformBufferReserve` defaults to `0` for the backend default; `reserveUniformBuffer(bytes)` sets a per-frame GPU uniform buffer reservation. Metal can grow the buffer, WebGPU and Vulkan require sufficient capacity, and GL and D3D11 ignore this reservation.

```cpp
int main() {
    WindowSettings settings;
    settings.setSize(1280, 720).setTitle("TrussC App").setHighDpi(true);
    return runApp<tcApp>(settings);
}
```

## WindowSettings::clipboardSize

- The default is 65536 bytes, including space for the terminating null character.
- On reads, macOS and Web truncate text to at most `clipboardSize - 1` bytes, while Windows fails UTF-8 conversion if the text does not fit.
- X11 rejects oversized or incremental clipboard transfers. The standalone backend returns an empty string, while the legacy backend returns null; `getClipboardString()` converts null to an empty string.
- On writes, macOS and Web send the full text to the system clipboard and truncate the local copy. Windows rejects text that exceeds its UTF-16 conversion buffer and truncates the local UTF-8 copy after a successful write.
- The standalone X11 backend rejects oversized writes; the legacy X11 backend logs an error and truncates the local copy.
- System clipboard access is unsupported on iOS and Android.

## WindowSettings::decorated

- The default is `true`; `false` hides the desktop window frame, title bar, and window buttons.
- A window without decorations can still receive keyboard focus and be closed programmatically.
- Web, iOS, and Android ignore this setting. The hot-reload launcher does not forward this setting.

## WindowSettings::fullscreen

- The default is `false`; `true` requests fullscreen when the main window starts.
- Secondary-window creation does not use this field.

## WindowSettings::height

- The default is `720`; see `WindowSettings::setSize` for size units and startup conversion.

## WindowSettings::highDpi

- The default is `true`, which requests a full-resolution framebuffer on high-DPI displays such as Retina.
- Disabling this setting requests a framebuffer at logical resolution. Coordinate units are controlled separately by `WindowSettings::pixelPerfect`.

## WindowSettings::pixelPerfect

- The default is `false`, which uses logical pixels for the main window's drawing and mouse coordinates. With `true`, these coordinates use framebuffer pixels.
- Startup size conversion is described in `WindowSettings::setSize`; high-DPI framebuffer allocation is controlled separately by `WindowSettings::highDpi`.
- The coordinate mode is shared across the app. Secondary-window creation ignores its own `pixelPerfect` value, and secondary-window mouse input always uses logical pixels.

## WindowSettings::reserveUniformBuffer

- `bytes` sets `uniformBufferReserve` in bytes and returns the same `WindowSettings&` for chaining. Set it before launching the app; graphics initialization reads the reservation once.
- A nonpositive value uses 1 MiB on Metal and 4 MiB on WebGPU or Vulkan. GL and D3D11 ignore this reservation because they do not use this per-frame uniform buffer limit.
- Budget the aligned size of every uniform upload. At 512 bytes per draw, 4 MiB holds about 8,000 draws and `reserveUniformBuffer(32 * 1024 * 1024)` holds about 65,000; leave headroom for larger shader blocks and other drawing.
- Alignment is 256 bytes on macOS Metal and the iOS simulator, 16 bytes on physical iOS devices, and device-dependent on WebGPU and Vulkan.
- Metal doubles the buffer capacity when it overflows and logs a warning; already encoded draws remain valid. Reserving enough capacity avoids these growth allocations.
- WebGPU does not grow the buffer: overflow triggers an assertion when assertions are enabled and can write beyond the CPU staging buffer when they are disabled. Vulkan logs an overflow error and skips affected draws.
- Larger reservations increase memory use without adding an allocation every frame. Metal and Vulkan allocate two buffers for frames in flight; WebGPU allocates a GPU buffer and CPU staging storage, each with an additional 64 KiB.
- The hot-reload launcher and secondary-window creation do not forward this reservation.

## WindowSettings::sampleCount

- The default is `4`; use `1` to disable multisample antialiasing.
- Supported counts depend on the device and backend. Desktop Linux with GLX chooses the closest supported count at startup, and secondary windows share that count.

## WindowSettings::setClipboardSize

- Stores `size` in `clipboardSize`, in bytes; see `WindowSettings::clipboardSize` for defaults and platform limits.
- Returns `WindowSettings&`; see `WindowSettings::setSize` for the shared setter rules.

## WindowSettings::setDecorated

- Stores `enabled` in `decorated`; see `WindowSettings::decorated` for appearance and platform behavior.
- Returns `WindowSettings&`; see `WindowSettings::setSize` for the shared setter rules.

## WindowSettings::setFullscreen

- Stores `enabled` in `fullscreen`; see `WindowSettings::fullscreen` for startup behavior.
- Returns `WindowSettings&`; see `WindowSettings::setSize` for the shared setter rules.

## WindowSettings::setHighDpi

- Stores `enabled` in `highDpi`; see `WindowSettings::highDpi` for framebuffer resolution behavior.
- Returns `WindowSettings&`; see `WindowSettings::setSize` for the shared setter rules.

## WindowSettings::setPixelPerfect

- Stores `enabled` in `pixelPerfect`; see `WindowSettings::pixelPerfect` for coordinate units and secondary-window behavior.
- Returns `WindowSettings&`; see `WindowSettings::setSize` for the shared setter rules.

## WindowSettings::setSampleCount

- Stores `count` in `sampleCount`; see `WindowSettings::sampleCount` for defaults and supported-count behavior.
- Returns `WindowSettings&`; see `WindowSettings::setSize` for the shared setter rules.

## WindowSettings::setSize

- Stores `w` and `h` in `width` and `height`. Main-window startup uses logical pixels when `pixelPerfect` is `false`; when it is `true`, startup divides each requested framebuffer dimension by `getDisplayScaleFactor()` and truncates to an integer before creating the window. This conversion also occurs when `highDpi` is `false`. Secondary-window creation always treats these dimensions as logical pixels.
- All `WindowSettings` setters assign values without validation and return a reference to the same settings object, so calls can be chained.
- Setters only change the settings object. Pass it to the launcher or window creation before the window is created; changing it afterward does not reconfigure that window. Use `setWindowSize()` to resize a running window.

```cpp
int main() {
    WindowSettings settings;
    settings.setSize(1280, 720).setTitle("Sketch");
    return TC_RUN_APP(tcApp, settings);
}
```

## WindowSettings::setSwapInterval

- Stores `interval` in `swapInterval`; see `WindowSettings::swapInterval` for refresh intervals and platform behavior, including how zero is handled.
- Returns `WindowSettings&`; see `WindowSettings::setSize` for the shared setter rules.

## WindowSettings::setTitle

- Copies `t` into `title`; see `WindowSettings::title` for the default and development-build title suffix.
- Returns `WindowSettings&`; see `WindowSettings::setSize` for the shared setter rules.

## WindowSettings::swapInterval

- The default is `1`, which synchronizes presentation to the display refresh. A supported positive value `N` requests presentation every `N` refreshes; for example, `2` requests 60 fps on a 120 Hz display.
- Zero is converted to `1` by the current desktop backends and the iOS defaults, so it does not disable VSync there. Web ignores this setting and uses browser animation-frame timing.
- On macOS and iOS, values above `1` also request a lower display-link rate. Only integer divisions of the refresh rate are expressible this way; use `setFps()` for other target frame rates.

## WindowSettings::title

- The default is `"TrussC App"`.
- Development builds append `" [MCP]"` to the main-window title unless it already contains `"[MCP]"`. Secondary-window titles use the supplied string directly.

## WindowSettings::uniformBufferReserve

- The default is `0`, which selects the backend default; positive values specify bytes.
- This is the backing field for `WindowSettings::reserveUniformBuffer`; see that entry for backend defaults, overflow behavior, memory cost, and startup restrictions.

## WindowSettings::width

- The default is `1280`; see `WindowSettings::setSize` for size units and startup conversion.

## WindowType

- `Rect` leaves samples unchanged; `Hanning`, `Hamming`, and `Blackman` weight samples with their respective cosine-based windows.
- Pass the value to `windowFunction()` for one coefficient or `applyWindow()` to multiply a signal in place. Window coefficients use normalized position `i / (n - 1)`; use at least two samples for the cosine-based windows.

## WritingMode

- `Horizontal` lays text out from left to right and is the default. `VerticalRL` lays glyphs out from top to bottom, with columns progressing from right to left.
- Select the mode with `Font::setWritingMode()`. Vertical layout uses `TcyMode` settings for Latin letter and digit runs.

## Xml

- Owns the XML document, which initially has no root element; use `root()`, `child()`, and `addRoot()` to access nodes as `XmlNode` handles.
- Node and attribute handles refer to document-owned data; destroying or resetting the document, replacing its contents during loading or parsing, or removing the corresponding nodes invalidates those handles.
- `load()` and `parse()` use the default pugixml options, which do not retain comments, processing instructions, XML declarations, document type declarations, or ordinary text nodes consisting only of literal XML whitespace. Whitespace from character references and whitespace inside CDATA are retained.
- `save()` and `toString()` output UTF-8 with two spaces per indentation level by default, and automatically include an XML declaration if the document has none.

## Xml::addDeclaration

- `addDeclaration(version, encoding)` adds a declaration with `version` and `encoding` attributes; the defaults are `"1.0"` and `"UTF-8"`.
- Always adds a new declaration, even if one already exists; returns no value.
- The encoding attribute does not change the UTF-8 output of `save()` or `toString()`; see `Xml` for serialization defaults.

## Xml::addRoot

- Appends an element named `name` directly to the document and returns it as an `XmlNode`.
- Does not replace an existing root element; repeated calls add more top-level elements.
- See `Xml` for node handle lifetime.

## Xml::child

- Returns the first direct child whose name exactly matches `name`, or an empty `XmlNode` if none matches.
- Searches the document itself, not inside its root element; use `root().child(name)` for a child of the root.
- See `Xml` for node handle lifetime.

## Xml::document

- Returns an `XmlDocument&`, or a `const XmlDocument&` when called on a const `Xml`, for operations through the pugixml API.
- Returns the owned document by reference without copying it; the reference is valid while its owning `Xml` exists.

## Xml::empty

- Returns `false` even for a newly constructed document with no content, because the underlying document handle exists.
- Use `!root()` to check whether there is no root element, or `!document().first_child()` to check whether the document has no child nodes.

## Xml::load

- Local input has no byte-size cap; documents above 16 MiB produce a Notice. Nesting is limited to 64 elements to keep DOM consumers safe. Parsing uses a temporary document; failure preserves the previous document and never publishes a parsed prefix.
- Accepts a file path; relative paths are resolved through `getDataPath()`, and absolute paths are used directly.
- Returns `true` on success and `false` for a missing or unreadable file or a parsing error; failures are logged, with a description and offset for parsing errors.
- See `Xml` for parsing defaults and node handle lifetime. Node handles remain valid after failure and are invalidated by a successful replacement.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    Xml xml;
    if (!xml.load("settings.xml")) return;
    logNotice() << xml.root().name();
}
```

## Xml::parse

- Local input has no byte-size cap; documents above 16 MiB produce a Notice. Nesting is limited to 64 elements to keep DOM consumers safe. Parsing uses a temporary document; failure preserves the previous document and never publishes a parsed prefix.
- Accepts a UTF-8 string; embedded null characters are rejected.
- Returns `true` on success; failure logs an error description and offset and returns `false`.
- See `Xml` for parsing defaults and node handle lifetime.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    Xml xml;
    if (!xml.parse("<settings><volume>0.5</volume></settings>")) return;
    logNotice() << xml.root().child("volume").text().as_float();
}
```

## Xml::root

- Returns the first top-level element as an `XmlNode`, skipping declarations and other non-element nodes; returns an empty handle if there is no element.
- Both const and non-const overloads return an `XmlNode` that can modify the element; see `Xml` for node handle lifetime.

## Xml::save

- `save(path, indent)` saves the entire document; `indent` is the per-level indentation string and defaults to two spaces. See `Xml` for serialization defaults.
- Returns a `SaveResult` that can be checked with `if (result)`; failures provide `error` and `message`, and serialization failures use `SaveError::WriteFailed`.
- Resolves relative paths through `getDataPath()`, uses absolute paths directly, and creates missing parent directories; paths inside the app bundle fail with `SaveError::AccessDenied`, so use `getUserDataPath()` for writable application data.
- Writes to `<file>.tmp`, checks writing and closing, then renames the temporary file over the destination; failures preserve the previous destination and attempt to remove the temporary file.
- Atomic replacement does not guarantee that the saved data survives power loss.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    Xml xml;
    xml.addRoot("settings").append_attribute("volume") = 0.5f;
    auto result = xml.save(getUserDataPath("settings.xml"));
    if (!result) logError() << result.message;
}
```

## Xml::toString

- Returns the entire document as a string without modifying it; `indent` sets the per-level indentation string and defaults to two spaces.
- See `Xml` for output encoding and automatic XML declaration behavior.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    auto xml = parseXml("<settings><volume>0.5</volume></settings>");
    string text = xml.toString("    ");
    logNotice() << text;
}
```

## XmlAttribute

- This is an alias for `pugi::xml_attribute` and uses the pugixml attribute API.
- Obtain an attribute with `node.attribute("name")` or create one with `node.append_attribute("name")`; read it with `value()` or conversion methods such as `as_int()`.
- A missing attribute is an empty handle that tests false; its `name()` and `value()` return empty strings.
- See `XmlDocument` for handle ownership and lifetime.

## XmlDocument

- This is an alias for `pugi::xml_document`, the owning document type used by `Xml`; `xml.document()` provides direct access to it.
- Use the pugixml API to load, query, edit, and save the tree; `reset()` removes its contents.
- Nodes and attributes are non-owning handles. Keep their document alive, and stop using affected handles after removing their contents, resetting the document, or loading replacement contents.
- Documents cannot be copied by assignment or a copy constructor; `reset(other)` replaces the contents with a copy of another document.

## XmlNode

- This is an alias for `pugi::xml_node`, returned by `Xml::root()` and `Xml::child()`.
- Use the pugixml node API, including `child()` for named children, `attribute()` for attributes, and `children()` for iteration.
- A failed child lookup returns an empty handle that tests false.
- See `XmlDocument` for handle ownership and lifetime.

## XmlParseResult

- This is an alias for `pugi::xml_parse_result`, returned by document methods such as `load_string()` and `load_file()`; `Xml::parse()` and `Xml::load()` return only a boolean.
- `if (result)` succeeds only when `status` is `pugi::status_ok`; `description()` returns a readable status description. A default-constructed result represents failure.
- `offset` records the error position from the start of the converted parsing buffer in `pugi::char_t` code units (UTF-8 bytes in the default build), and is normally zero on success. `encoding` records the source encoding.

## abs

- `abs(x)` returns the magnitude of `x`; for example, `abs(-2.5f)` returns `2.5f`. A `float` argument produces a `float` result.
- This is a standard-library function, available unqualified with `using namespace std;`, rather than a member of `tc`.

## acos

- The standard-library function `acos(x)` returns an angle in radians in the range `[0, TAU / 2]` for `x` in `[-1, 1]`.
- Inputs outside `[-1, 1]` cause a domain error; no clamping is applied.

## addLight

- Accepts a `Light&` and registers its address for subsequent lighting. Each window holds up to eight lights; adding the same object again does nothing, and additions beyond eight are ignored with a one-time warning.
- Registration does not copy or own the light. Keep its address stable, for example as an application member; copying a light does not register the copy, and moving it does not transfer registration.
- Changes to the registered object are read by subsequent draws. Destroying it removes its registration from all window contexts; `removeLight` and `clearLights` affect only the current window.
- Registering lights alone does not enable PBR mesh rendering; use `setMaterial` with a mesh that has normals.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    static Light light;
    light.setDirectional(0, -1, -1);
    addLight(light);
}
```

## alertDialog

- `alertDialog(title, message)` displays a heading or title and body text with an OK button on supported platforms, returning after dismissal.
- Synchronous dialogs run on the calling thread and do not dispatch to the main thread. Call them from a main-thread app callback; the caller waits while the dialog is open.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    alertDialog("Welcome", "Press OK to continue.");
}
```

## alertDialogAsync

- `alertDialogAsync(title, message, callback)` displays a heading and body text; the optional `void()` callback defaults to `nullptr` and is called after dismissal or completion of the platform fallback.
- Call the Async dialog family on the main thread; macOS and iOS deliver callbacks on the main thread, while Windows, Linux, Android, and Web invoke them on the calling thread without starting a worker.
- Async does not guarantee a deferred callback: Windows, Linux, and Web block until their supported dialogs close, Android completes immediately, and macOS blocks when there is no key window; callbacks can run before the function returns.
- On macOS and iOS, callbacks are delivered only while the app run that requested them remains active; ending that run or replacing it during hot reload suppresses pending callbacks.
- On iOS, a missing root view controller logs an error and invokes the callback without showing a dialog.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    alertDialogAsync("Notice", "Settings loaded.", []() {
        logNotice() << "Alert completed";
    });
}
```

## angleDifference

- `angleDifference(angle1, angle2)` reduces `angle2 - angle1` to the range `[-TAU / 2, TAU / 2]` and returns a `float`.
- At exactly half a turn, the sign of the remainder is preserved; `angleDifference(0, TAU / 2)` is positive, and reversing the arguments makes it negative.

## angleDifferenceDeg

- `angleDifferenceDeg(deg1, deg2)` reduces `deg2 - deg1` to the range `[-180, 180]` and returns a `float`.
- At exactly half a turn, the sign of the remainder is preserved; `angleDifferenceDeg(0, 180)` returns 180, and reversing the arguments returns -180.

## appendArc

- Adds the points of an arc to the shape you are building between `beginShape()` and `endShape()`. It does not draw anything by itself.
- The arguments are the same as for `drawArc`: center, radius, start angle and end angle in radians. See `drawArc` for the angle direction and `drawRect` for coordinates.
- Both end points of the arc are added. Unlike `drawArc`, no center point is added, so you decide how to close the arc: as a chord, as a pie slice (add the center with `vertex()` yourself), or as part of a larger outline. `drawRectRounded` builds its corners this way.
- The number of points follows `setCurveResolution` or `setCurveTolerance`. It also works inside `beginStroke()` and `beginLines()`, because it adds the points with `vertex()`.
- If the previous point is already at the start of the arc, the repeated point does no harm.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    setColor(0.2f, 0.8f, 1.0f);
    beginShape();
    vertex(200, 200);                       // center
    appendArc(200, 200, 80, 0, HALF_TAU);   // rim points of the half-arc
    endShape(true);                         // close back to center
}
```

## appendCurve

- Adds the points of a smooth Catmull-Rom curve to the buffer that is open: `beginShape`, `beginStroke` or `beginLines`. The result is the same as calling `vertex()` in a loop. The curve is the same kind as `drawCurve` draws.

```cpp
beginShape();
vertex(20, 150);
appendCurve({Vec3(20,150,0), Vec3(80,30,0), Vec3(200,30,0),
             Vec3(260,150,0)});
endShape();
```

- `appendCurve(points)` needs at least 4 points. With fewer, it does nothing. The curve passes through the inner points only. The first and last points only set the direction at the ends and are not added as vertices.
- `appendCurve(points, true)` makes a closed curve. It needs at least 3 points and passes through all of them.
- How smooth the curve is depends on `setCurveResolution` or `setCurveTolerance`.
- To protect CPU and memory from very large input, arrays of more than 100,000 points are refused with a warning. The program does not crash.

## appendSuperellipse

- Adds the closed outline of a superellipse to the shape you are building between `beginShape()` and `endShape()`. It does not draw anything by itself.
- The arguments are the same as for `drawSuperellipse`: a rectangle `(x, y, w, h)` with its top-left corner at `(x, y)`, and the exponent `n`. See `drawRect` for coordinates.
- The start point is added twice to close the loop. The repeated point does no harm.
- `endShape()` fills with triangles that start from the first point, so the fill is correct only for convex outlines (`n >= 1`). For concave shapes (`n < 1`), use `drawSuperellipse` instead, which fills them correctly.

## appendToFile

- `appendToFile(path, content)` appends all bytes of `content` in binary mode, preserving line endings and embedded null bytes. It creates the file if it does not exist and does not add a newline.
- Returns `SaveResult` after checking the write, flush, and close. Failures are logged as Error; writing occurs directly in the destination, so a failure can leave partially appended data.
- For relative-path resolution, missing parent directories, and app-bundle restrictions, see `saveTextFile`. For boolean conversion, see `SaveResult`; for streaming output and its failure handling, see `FileWriter`.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    auto result = appendToFile(getUserDataPath("events.txt"), "Started\n");
    if (!result) logError() << result.message;
}
```

## applyWindow

- `applyWindow(signal, type)` multiplies each sample by a window coefficient to reduce spectral leakage before an FFT. It accepts `vector<float>` or `vector<complex<float>>` and returns no value.
- `type` is required. `WindowType::Rect` uses a coefficient of `1`; complex samples have both components multiplied by the same real coefficient. The vector length is unchanged.
- Empty input is unchanged. Coefficient formulas and the one-sample limitation are described in `windowFunction`.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    vector<float> signal(1024, 1.0f);
    applyWindow(signal, WindowType::Hanning);
    auto spectrum = fftReal(signal);
}
```

## asin

- The standard-library function `asin(x)` returns an angle in radians in the range `[-TAU / 4, TAU / 4]` for `x` in `[-1, 1]`.
- Inputs outside `[-1, 1]` cause a domain error; no clamping is applied.

## atan

- The standard-library function `atan(x)` accepts a tangent value and returns an angle in radians; finite inputs produce a result in `[-TAU / 4, TAU / 4]`, including endpoints due to rounding.
- Use `atan2(y, x)` when both vector components are available and the quadrant must be preserved.

## atan2

- The standard-library function `atan2(y, x)` takes the vertical component first and returns the angle from the positive X axis in radians in `[-TAU / 2, TAU / 2]`.
- Both signs determine the quadrant, and `x` may be zero; there is no need to divide `y` by `x` first.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    Vec2 direction(1.0f, 1.0f);
    float angle = atan2(direction.y, direction.x);
}
```

## audio::priority::Effect

- This integer constant is `500`; pass it as the priority argument to `AudioEngine::audioOut.listen(...)` for effects that read and modify the audio buffer.
- Effects run after `audio::priority::Generator` and before `audio::priority::Monitor`. See `audio::priority::Generator` for shared ordering and callback rules.

## audio::priority::Generator

- This integer constant is `100`, equal to `EventPriority::App` and the default listener priority. Use it for listeners that generate audio into the output buffer.
- `AudioEngine::audioOut` listeners run in ascending numeric priority: Generator (`100`), Effect (`500`), then Monitor (`900`). Equal priorities run in registration order; intermediate values allow additional stages.
- These listeners run after the engine mixes `Sound` voices. Default inline callbacks run on the audio thread in native builds and on the browser main thread in default Web builds, and share the output buffer; see `App::audioOut` for audio callback restrictions, and retain the returned `EventListener`.

## audio::priority::Monitor

- This integer constant is `900`; use it for monitoring, scopes, FFT analysis, or recording listeners that should observe the buffer after effects.
- It runs after the predefined Generator and Effect priorities. Reading without modifying the buffer is a usage convention; see `audio::priority::Generator` for shared ordering and callback rules.

## beep

- Call `beep()` for the default `Beep::ping`, `beep(Beep::success)` for a preset, or `beep(440.0f)` for a sine tone with a frequency in hertz.
- All presets and frequencies share a 5 ms suppression interval across windows; calls within 5 ms of the last accepted call do nothing.
- Sounds are generated on the CPU when first needed and cached. Frequencies share a cache entry when conversion to `int` gives the same value, so the first frequency used for that entry determines its pitch.
- Playing a cached sound restarts it; different cached sounds can overlap. Adding a new entry when the cache already contains 128 entries clears the cache and stops its sounds.
- The initial volume is `0.5f`. The cache, volume, and suppression interval are shared across the process and survive hot reloads.
- Sound generation initializes the audio engine if needed. Playback starts asynchronously, and this function returns no success or failure value; see `Sound` for playback failure conditions.
- Calls to `beep`, `setBeepVolume`, and `getBeepVolume` are not synchronized. Use one thread or provide external synchronization.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    setBeepVolume(0.3f);
    beep(Beep::success);
}
```

## beginLines

- Opens a buffer for drawing many **separate line segments** at once. Add points with `vertex()` and call `endLines()` to draw them. Nothing is drawn before `endLines()`.
- Points are used **in pairs**. Points 0 and 1 make the first segment, points 2 and 3 make the second, and so on. A last point without a partner is ignored, and at least 2 points are needed.
- Each point stores the color that is set when its `vertex()` is called. Set the color between points to color each segment, or each end of a segment for a gradient.

```cpp
beginLines();
setColor(colors::red);    vertex(20, 20);
setColor(colors::blue);   vertex(200, 80);   // segment 1: red to blue
setColor(colors::lime);   vertex(20, 120);
setColor(colors::yellow); vertex(200, 180);  // segment 2: lime to yellow
endLines();
```

- The lines are thin (1px) and do not follow the stroke weight. For thick lines with caps and joins, use `beginStroke`. For one connected line, use `beginShape` with `noFill`.

## beginShadowPass

- Before PBR drawing, call `beginShadowPass(light)`, draw each caster with `shadowDraw(mesh)`, and call `endShadowPass()`. Repeat for each shadow-casting light.
- The light must be registered with `addLight` in the current window; an unregistered light does nothing. Directional lights use their shadow-area orthographic view, and spot lights use their perspective view; point lights are ignored with a one-time warning.
- The function does not check `isShadowEnabled()`: calling `disableShadow()` alone does not prevent an explicitly requested pass.
- Each window allows up to four shadow passes per frame, each using a separate array layer. Repeating the same light consumes another layer; passes beyond four are ignored with a one-time warning.
- All layers share a resolution that grows to the largest shadow resolution requested by a light passed here and does not shrink. Increasing it recreates the array, so render lights requesting the largest resolution first.
- The pair can run inside an Fbo. It inherits the caller's model transform; ending resumes the original color and depth attachments and restores the caller's transforms, viewport, and clipping.
- Nested shadow passes are rejected with a warning. If the shadow shader is unavailable, no pass starts; outside an active pass, `shadowDraw()` and `endShadowPass()` do nothing.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    static Light light;
    light.enableShadow(1024);
    addLight(light);
    Mesh mesh = createBox(100);
    beginShadowPass(light);
    shadowDraw(mesh); endShadowPass();
}
```

## beginShape

- Use it to draw your own polygon. Call `beginShape()`, add points with `vertex()`, and finish with `endShape()`. `endShape()` draws the polygon and empties the buffer.
- Coordinates and units are the same as for `drawRect`.
- You can add any number of points. You can also add curved parts with `appendArc` and `appendCurve`.

```cpp
beginShape();
vertex(100, 50);
vertex(150, 150);
vertex(50, 150);
endShape(true);   // true closes the outline back to the first vertex
```

- Shapes cannot be nested. If you call `beginShape()` again before `endShape()`, the points added so far are discarded.

## beginStroke

- Draws a connected line with **width, end caps and corner joins**. The outline of `beginShape` is always a thin 1px line, but this one follows the stroke settings.
- Set the look with `setStrokeWeight`, `setStrokeCap` and `setStrokeJoin`, add points with `vertex()`, and finish with `endStroke()`.

```cpp
setStrokeWeight(8);
setStrokeCap(StrokeCap::Round);
setStrokeJoin(StrokeJoin::Round);
beginStroke();
vertex(50, 50);
vertex(150, 80);
vertex(250, 50);
endStroke();        // open line; pass true to close it into a loop
```

- Each `vertex()` stores the **current stroke weight**. Calling `setStrokeWeight` between points changes the width along the line.
- The cap is the `setStrokeCap` value that is set when the **first** point is added. It is used at both ends, and changing it later has no effect on this stroke. The join is the `setStrokeJoin` value that is set when `endStroke()` is called.
- The whole stroke is drawn in one color, the color of the **first** point. Calling `setColor()` between points does not make a gradient. Use `beginLines` for colors that change per segment.
- Internally it builds a `StrokeMesh`.

## binToFrequency

- `binToFrequency(bin, fftSize, sampleRate)` returns `(float)bin * sampleRate / fftSize` in Hz. `fftSize` is the full transform length, and `sampleRate` is the sampling rate in samples per second.
- The index is not clamped, and upper bins are not converted to negative frequencies. Supply a positive `fftSize`; zero is not checked.

## bindCursorImage

- Pass `cursor, width, height, pixels` with tightly packed RGBA8 data containing `width * height * 4` bytes, or pass `cursor, image`; the `Image` overload forwards its CPU pixels without converting the channel count or format.
- `hotspotX` and `hotspotY` specify the click point in image pixels from the top-left corner and both default to zero.
- Bind a slot such as `Cursor::Custom0` through `Cursor::Custom15`, then select it with `setCursor`; binding replaces the slot's previous image and immediately updates it if selected. `unbindCursorImage` releases the binding.
- Desktop and Web implementations copy the supplied pixels during the call; the binding belongs to the main-window cursor rather than the current secondary window. Custom cursor creation is unavailable on iOS and Android, and this function returns no success status.

## bringWindowToFront

- Targets the main application window, including when called from a secondary window; macOS activates the application, Windows requests foreground activation, and Linux raises the X11 window and requests input focus.
- Returns no success status and does nothing if the required native window or Linux display connection is unavailable.

## bytesPerPixel

- Returns an `int`: `R8` is 1; `RG8` and `R16F` are 2; `RGBA8`, `BGRA8`, `RG16F`, and `R32F` are 4; `RGBA16`, `RGBA16F`, and `RG32F` are 8; `RGBA32F` is 16.
- Unrecognized values return `4`. This function accepts `TextureFormat`, not `PixelFormat` or compressed sokol formats.
- See `TextureFormat` for channel layouts and component types.

## calculateLighting

- Accepts `worldPos`, `worldNormal`, and a `Material`; provide a normalized world-space normal because the function does not normalize it.
- Sums enabled registered lights in the current window and uses the current render target's camera position for specular reflections.
- Uses a Phong approximation derived from the material's base color, metallic value, and roughness. Spot lights are treated as point lights without cone falloff; textures, IES profiles, shadows, environment lighting, and material ambient occlusion are not evaluated.
- If no lights are registered, returns the material base color directly, ignoring emission. Otherwise, starts with emissive color multiplied by emissive strength and adds the light contributions; if all registered lights are disabled, only emission remains.
- Each light adds ambient, diffuse, and specular terms; intensity and distance attenuation affect diffuse and specular terms, but not ambient.
- With a nonempty light list, limits each resulting RGB channel to a maximum of `1` without enforcing a minimum, and preserves the material base-color alpha. The function returns a `Color` without drawing or reading GPU pixels.

## captureWindow

- `captureWindow(outPixels)` fills a `Pixels` object with RGBA8 data at the source framebuffer's physical pixel dimensions, with the top row first; it returns `true` on success and `false` on failure.
- Captures the current window's rendered contents; call from `draw()` or an `events().afterFrame` listener with a valid graphics context. Native implementations return `false` while an `Fbo` begun with `begin()` has not yet been ended with `end()`.
- Readback is synchronous and can stall rendering while GPU work completes; macOS returns `false` if completion takes longer than ten seconds.
- Output contents are not guaranteed to remain unchanged on failure; use the pixels only after a successful return.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    drawCircle(100.0f, 100.0f, 40.0f);
    Pixels pixels;
    if (captureWindow(pixels)) {
        logNotice() << pixels.getWidth() << " x " << pixels.getHeight();
    }
}
```

## ceil

- The standard-library function `ceil(x)` returns the smallest integer value greater than or equal to `x`; for example, `ceil(-1.2f)` returns `-1.0f`.
- A `float` argument produces a `float` result, not an integer type.

## channelCount

- Returns an `int`: `R8`, `R16F`, and `R32F` return `1`; `RG8`, `RG16F`, and `RG32F` return `2`; all other defined TextureFormat values return `4`.
- Unrecognized values also return `4`; see `TextureFormat` for channel layouts.

## clamp

- `clamp(value, min, max)` takes and returns `float` values; values below `min` become `min`, values above `max` become `max`, and values within the inclusive range are unchanged.
- Bounds are not reordered; if `min > max`, the function returns `min`.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    float opacity = clamp(1.2f, 0.0f, 1.0f);
}
```

## cleanup

- Releases rendering targets and bitmap font resources, submits pending renderer work without presenting it, and shuts down `sokol_gl` and `sokol_gfx`.
- The normal application loop calls this automatically after the application's exit and cleanup callbacks and audio shutdown; ordinary applications do not need to call it directly.
- This free function is separate from the overridable `Node::cleanup()` callback; see `App` and `Node` for application and node teardown.

## clear

- Repaints the whole active render target (the window, or the FBO currently bound with `beginFbo`) with a flat color, erasing anything drawn before it in that target this frame. If the target has a depth buffer, `clear()` also resets it, so 3D content drawn after `clear()` is never occluded by content drawn before it.
- No arguments: transparent black (0, 0, 0, 0).
- One or two arguments: grayscale, `clear(gray, a = 1)`.
- Three or four arguments, or a `Color`: `clear(r, g, b, a = 1)` / `clear(const Color&)`, all 0-1 floats.
- Typically called once at the top of `draw()`; calling it again mid-frame still works, but paints over whatever was already drawn to that target.
- Does nothing in headless mode, since there is no graphics context to clear.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    clear(colors::black);   // paint the whole window black
    setColor(colors::white);
    drawCircle(getWidth() / 2, getHeight() / 2, 40);
}
```

## clearEnvironment

- Sets the current window's environment pointer to `nullptr`; subsequent PBR mesh draws use the ambient fallback described under `Environment`.
- Does not release the previously selected object's textures or change other windows' selections.
- Threading and ownership rules are described under `Environment`.

## clearLights

- Empties the current window's light list without destroying or changing the Light objects; `getNumLights()` then returns `0`.
- Registration and lifetime rules are described in `addLight`.

## clearMaterial

- Clears the selected material without destroying it, so subsequent ordinary `Mesh::draw()` calls use rendering without lighting.
- This function does not restore a previously selected material. Material selection and lifetime are described in `setMaterial`.

## closeLogFile

- Calls `getLogger().closeFile()` and clears its stored file path; calling it without an open file is safe.
- Returns no value; a close failure is reported at Error level directly to console and system outputs, subject to their thresholds.
- Console output, system output and `onLog` remain active; see `Logger` for threading rules.

## colorFromHSB

- `colorFromHSB(h, s, b, a = 1.0f)` returns exactly the same result as `Color::fromHSB(h, s, b, a)`.
- Hue uses 0–1 for one turn; saturation, brightness, and alpha normally use 0–1. For conversion and hue wrapping behavior, see `ColorHSB`.
- This backward-compatible alias is deprecated and scheduled for removal in v1.0.0. Use `Color::fromHSB()` in new code.

## colorFromLinear

- `colorFromLinear(r, g, b, a = 1.0f)` returns exactly the same result as `Color::fromLinear(r, g, b, a)`.
- RGB arguments are linear values; sRGB encoding is applied to RGB while alpha is preserved. For component ranges and conversion behavior, see `ColorLinear`.
- This backward-compatible alias is deprecated and scheduled for removal in v1.0.0. Use `Color::fromLinear()` in new code.

## colorFromOKLCH

- `colorFromOKLCH(L, C, H, a = 1.0f)` returns exactly the same result as `Color::fromOKLCH(L, C, H, a)`.
- Arguments specify lightness, chroma, hue, and alpha; hue uses 0–1 for one turn. For component ranges and conversion behavior, see `ColorOKLCH`.
- This backward-compatible alias is deprecated and scheduled for removal in v1.0.0. Use `Color::fromOKLCH()` in new code.

## colorFromOKLab

- `colorFromOKLab(L, a_lab, b_lab, alpha = 1.0f)` returns exactly the same result as `Color::fromOKLab(L, a_lab, b_lab, alpha)`.
- Arguments specify lightness, two opponent color axes, and alpha; `a_lab` is a color axis, not alpha. For component ranges and conversion behavior, see `ColorOKLab`.
- This backward-compatible alias is deprecated and scheduled for removal in v1.0.0. Use `Color::fromOKLab()` in new code.

## compress

- Pass `src`, its size `nbytes` in bytes, and an explicit `codec`; `Codec::LZ4` performs lossless block compression, while `Codec::None` copies the bytes unchanged.
- The vector overload `compress(src, nbytes, out, codec)` resizes `out` to the compressed size and returns `true`; on compression failure it clears `out` and returns `false`.
- The raw overload `compress(src, nbytes, dst, dstCapacity, codec)` writes into caller-owned storage without resizing it and returns the number of bytes written as `int`, or `-1` on failure, including insufficient capacity or an unsupported codec. For `Codec::None`, keep `nbytes` representable as `int`; larger copies do not reliably return their byte count or `-1`.
- Use `compressBound(nbytes, codec)` to size a raw destination buffer. LZ4 rejects input larger than 2,113,929,216 bytes and casts `dstCapacity` to `int`; keep the capacity representable as `int`.
- Use non-overlapping source and destination storage; in particular, do not use storage owned by `out` as the source of the vector overload, because `out` is resized before the input is read.
- Compression does not store the codec or original byte count; retain both for `decompress()`.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    vector<uint8_t> data = {1, 2, 3, 4};
    vector<uint8_t> packed;
    if (!compress(data.data(), data.size(), packed, Codec::LZ4)) {
        logError() << "Compression failed";
    }
}
```

## compressBound

- Pass the uncompressed byte count `nbytes` and an explicit `codec`; the returned `size_t` is the destination capacity to reserve for raw `compress()`.
- `Codec::None` returns `nbytes`; `Codec::LZ4` returns the LZ4 compression bound. An unsupported codec returns `0`.
- For LZ4, keep `nbytes` within 0–2,113,929,216 bytes. The implementation casts it to `int` before calculating the bound and returns `0` if that converted value is outside the supported LZ4 range.

## confirmDialog

- `confirmDialog(title, message)` displays a title and body text. Returns `true` for an affirmative choice and `false` for rejection or failure.
- Threading and blocking behavior follow `alertDialog`.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    if (confirmDialog("Continue", "Start the sketch?")) {
        logNotice() << "Confirmed";
    }
}
```

## confirmDialogAsync

- `confirmDialogAsync(title, message, callback)` displays a heading and body text and supplies the result to a `void(bool)` callback; all arguments are required.
- The callback receives `true` for Yes or browser OK, and `false` for No, cancellation, or failure.
- On iOS, a missing root view controller logs an error and invokes the callback with `false`.
- See `alertDialogAsync` for shared threading, callback timing, and app run lifetime rules.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    confirmDialogAsync("Continue", "Load the settings?", [](bool accepted) {
        if (accepted) logNotice() << "Confirmed";
    });
}
```

## cos

- The standard-library function `cos(x)` takes an angle in radians and returns a value in `[-1, 1]` for finite input; one full turn is `TAU`.
- A `float` argument produces a `float` result.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    float angle = TAU / 8.0f;
    Vec2 direction(cos(angle), sin(angle));
}
```

## createBox

- `createBox(width, height, depth)` creates a box centered at the origin with dimensions along X, Y, and Z; `createBox(size)` creates a cube.
- Contains 24 vertices and 12 triangles, with separate vertices, outward normals, and 0–1 texture coordinates for each face.
- All primitive generators in this group return a new indexed `Mesh` in `PrimitiveMode::Triangles`. They generate CPU data without drawing or uploading it to the GPU; lengths use mesh coordinates. See `Mesh` for drawing.
- Dimensions are used without validation.

```cpp
// tcApp.h: Mesh mesh;
void tcApp::setup() {
    mesh = createBox(100.0f, 60.0f, 40.0f);
}
```

## createCapsule

- `createCapsule(radius, cylinderHeight, resolution = 16)` creates a capsule centered at the origin along the Y axis.
- `cylinderHeight` is the length of the straight cylindrical section; total height is `cylinderHeight + 2 * radius`.
- `resolution` controls the number of sectors around the axis. Each hemisphere uses `max(2, resolution / 2)` rings with integer division; the sector count is not clamped or validated.
- Generates normals, texture coordinates, and tangents. Mesh generation and length units follow `createBox`.

## createCone

- `createCone(radius, height, resolution = 16)` creates a Y-axis cone with its base at `y = -height / 2` and its tip at `y = height / 2`.
- `radius` is the base radius, `height` is the full height, and `resolution` is the number of sectors around the axis; the sector count is not clamped or validated.
- Includes a bottom cap and texture coordinates. Each side triangle has separate vertices with a constant normal; the cap normals point toward −Y.
- Mesh generation and length units follow `createBox`.

## createCylinder

- `createCylinder(radius, height, resolution = 16)` creates a capped cylinder centered at the origin along the Y axis, extending from `-height / 2` to `height / 2`.
- `resolution` is the number of sectors around the axis; it is not clamped or validated.
- Generates texture coordinates and separate vertices for the sides and caps. Side normals point radially outward, and cap normals point toward +Y and −Y.
- Mesh generation and length units follow `createBox`.

## createDirectory

- Resolves `path` through `getDataPath()` and creates missing directories recursively; see `getDataPath` for path-resolution rules.
- Returns `true` if the directory is created or already exists, and `false` if an existing item is not a directory. Filesystem exceptions during the existence check or creation are logged as Error and return `false`.

## createIcoSphere

- `createIcoSphere(radius, subdivisions = 2)` creates a sphere centered at the origin with approximately even triangle sizes.
- Each subdivision splits every triangle into four and projects new vertices onto the sphere. The default produces 320 triangles; zero or negative subdivisions leave the original 20-triangle icosahedron.
- Generates outward vertex normals but no texture coordinates or tangents.
- Mesh generation and length units follow `createBox`.

## createPlane

- `createPlane(width, height, cols = 2, rows = 2)` creates a rectangle centered at the origin at `z = 0`, with width along X and height along Y.
- `cols` and `rows` are cell counts, producing `(cols + 1) * (rows + 1)` vertices and `2 * cols * rows` triangles. The defaults produce 9 vertices and 8 triangles.
- Generates +Z normals and 0–1 texture coordinates. Triangle winding faces −Z.
- Cell counts are not clamped or validated; zero counts cause division by zero during generation. Mesh generation and length units follow `createBox`.

```cpp
// tcApp.h: Mesh mesh;
void tcApp::setup() {
    mesh = createPlane(200.0f, 100.0f, 10, 5);
}
```

## createSphere

- `createSphere(radius, resolution = 16)` creates a sphere centered at the origin, with its poles on the Y axis.
- `resolution` controls both latitude and longitude divisions; it is not clamped or validated.
- Generates outward normals, 0–1 texture coordinates, and tangents. Vertices are duplicated at the longitude seam, and degenerate triangles at the poles are omitted.
- Mesh generation and length units follow `createBox`.

```cpp
// tcApp.h: Mesh mesh;
void tcApp::setup() {
    mesh = createSphere(50.0f, 32);
}
```

## createTorus

- `createTorus(radius, tubeRadius, sides = 24, rings = 16)` creates a torus centered at the origin around the Y axis, with its main circle on the XZ plane.
- `radius` is the distance from the origin to the tube center, and `tubeRadius` is the tube cross-section radius; the outer radius is `radius + tubeRadius`.
- `sides` divides the tube cross-section, and `rings` divides the main circle. Neither count is clamped or validated.
- Generates outward normals and 0–1 texture coordinates, duplicating vertices at both seams. Mesh generation and length units follow `createBox`.

## decompress

- Pass the compressed buffer `src`, its byte count `nbytes`, and the codec used by `compress()`; `Codec::None` copies the input unchanged.
- The vector overload `decompress(src, nbytes, out, decompressedSize, codec)` requires the known original byte count, resizes `out` to that size, and returns `true` only when exactly that many bytes are produced. Failure or a size mismatch clears `out` and returns `false`.
- The raw overload `decompress(src, nbytes, dst, dstCapacity, codec)` writes into caller-owned storage and returns the number of bytes written as `int`, or `-1` on failure. A result smaller than `dstCapacity` is allowed; this overload does not check the expected original size. Inputs whose byte count cannot be represented as `int` return `-1`.
- The vector overload checks encoded lengths and proves the exact LZ4 output size before allocation. Output has no policy cap; LZ4 output over 256 MiB emits one Notice. It logs an Error on failure. The raw overload has no output policy cap; it checks that `nbytes` fits `int` and clamps LZ4 `dstCapacity` to `INT_MAX` before decoding.
- For source and destination storage rules, see `compress`.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    vector<uint8_t> data = {1, 2, 3, 4};
    vector<uint8_t> packed, restored;
    if (compress(data.data(), data.size(), packed, Codec::LZ4)) {
        if (!decompress(packed.data(), packed.size(), restored, data.size(), Codec::LZ4))
            logError() << "Decompression failed";
    }
}
```

## deg2rad

- Takes a `float` angle in degrees and returns `deg * TAU / 360` as a `float`; it does not wrap the angle.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    Vec2 direction = Vec2(1.0f, 0.0f).rotated(deg2rad(90.0f));
}
```

## directoryExists

- Resolves `path` through `getDataPath()` and returns `true` only if it exists and is a directory; see `getDataPath` for path-resolution rules.
- Filesystem query errors can throw exceptions; they are not converted to `false` or logged by this function.

## disableDepthTest

- Call it before drawing 2D overlays such as a HUD or text after a 3D scene, so the scene does not hide them.
- It takes effect immediately, even inside an `EasyCam` scope: drawing after it no longer tests or writes depth.
- The setting stays off across frames and `Fbo` passes until `enableDepthTest()` is called again.
- How the depth test works and when it is needed are explained in `enableDepthTest`.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    cam.begin();
    setBlendMode(BlendMode::Add);
    enableDepthTest();
    drawSphere(0, 0, 0, 50);
    resetBlendMode();
    cam.end();
    disableDepthTest();                       // 2D from here is never hidden by the scene
    drawBitmapString("score: 10", 20, 20);
}
```

## disable3D

- Calls `setupScreenOrtho()` with identical behavior; use that function in new code and refer to it for projection behavior.
- Scheduled for removal in v1.0.0.

## dist

- Accepts four `float` coordinates as `dist(x1, y1, x2, y2)`, two `Vec2` values, or two `Vec3` values, and returns a `float` distance.
- Calculates the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences; coincident points return zero.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    float distance = dist(Vec2(0.0f, 0.0f), Vec2(3.0f, 4.0f));
}
```

## distSquared

- Accepts four `float` coordinates as `distSquared(x1, y1, x2, y2)`, two `Vec2` values, or two `Vec3` values, and returns the sum of squared coordinate differences as a `float`.
- Avoids calculating a square root; for a nonnegative radius `r`, compare the result with `sq(r)` to test distance against that radius.

## drawArc

- Draws part of a circle with center `(x, y)` and the given `radius`, from `angleBegin` to `angleEnd`. A `Vec3 center` version is also available for 3D.
- Angles are in **radians**, not degrees. Use `TAU`, `HALF_TAU` and `QUARTER_TAU`. For example, `drawArc(x, y, r, 0, HALF_TAU)` draws a semicircle.
- `0` points to the right. Because `y` grows downward on screen, a larger angle moves clockwise on screen, and `QUARTER_TAU` points down.
- The arc covers `angleEnd - angleBegin`. It does not wrap around at `TAU`. For example, from `5.5` to `0.5` the arc goes backward by `5.0` radians.
- With `noFill()`, only the open curve is drawn. With `fill()`, the arc is closed to the center and filled as a pie slice, like in p5.js and Processing. This is the only shape in this group where the filled area and the outline do not follow the same edge.
- For a different closed shape, such as a chord or a custom outline, call `appendArc` between `beginShape()` and `endShape()`. `appendArc` adds only the points on the arc, not the center.
- The number of segments follows the current curve settings. You can change them with `setCurveTolerance` or `setCurveResolution`.
- Nothing is drawn when `radius <= 0` or when `angleBegin == angleEnd`.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    setColor(1.0f, 0.6f, 0.1f);
    fill();
    drawArc(200, 200, 80, 0, HALF_TAU);   // filled half pie: from right, through bottom, to left
}
```

## drawBezier

- `drawBezier(p0, p1, p2, p3)` draws a cubic Bezier curve with 4 control points. `drawBezier(p0, p1, p2)` draws a quadratic curve with 3 control points. The curve starts at the first point and ends at the last one.

```cpp
drawBezier(Vec3(50, 150, 0), Vec3(100, 20, 0),
           Vec3(200, 20, 0), Vec3(250, 150, 0));
```

- `drawBezier(vector<Vec3>)` takes any number of control points and draws a curve of higher order. With fewer than 2 points it draws nothing. With 2 points it draws a straight line, and with 3 or 4 points it uses the quadratic or cubic version above.
- `drawBezier` always draws a thin 1px line, like `drawLine`. It ignores `fill()` and `noFill()` and the stroke weight, because an open curve has no inside to fill.
- For a filled curved shape or a thick curve, build the points with `Path::bezierTo`, or pass sampled points to `beginStroke`.
- The curve is drawn as many short line segments. Their number follows the current curve settings, which you can change with `setCurveTolerance` or `setCurveResolution`.
- In the default Tolerance mode, the vector version accepts at most 64 control points. With more points it prints a warning and draws nothing. In that case, join several cubic curves instead.

## drawBitmapString

- Draws `text` using the built-in bitmap font. Each ASCII character occupies an 8x16 pixel cell (a 13-pixel-tall glyph plus padding); non-ASCII characters use their own registered width, falling back to a half-width placeholder glyph when not registered. The position (x, y) follows the same coordinate conventions as other 2D drawing — see `drawRect` for the basics.
- Printable ASCII (`U+0020`–`U+007E`) always uses the built-in glyphs, even after `bitmapfont::registerGlyph()`; use a non-ASCII codepoint such as `U+E000` for a custom glyph.
- By default (`screenFixed = true`, used by `(text, x, y)` and `(text, x, y, screenFixed)`), the glyph size stays fixed in pixels and ignores any rotation or scale from `pushMatrix`; only the position moves with the current matrix. Pass `screenFixed = false`, or use the `(text, x, y, scale)` overload, to make the text rotate and scale together with the current transform.
- A newline (`\n`) starts a new line. The spacing between lines defaults to the font height (`getBitmapFontHeight()`) and can be changed with `setBitmapLineHeight()`. A tab (`\t`) advances by 8 character widths.
- The anchor point used for (x, y) is controlled by `setTextAlign()`; see that entry for the available alignments and what they affect.
- Fill and stroke settings have no effect on bitmap text: it is always drawn filled, using the current drawing color set by `setColor()`.
- For multi-line text, a center or right horizontal alignment aligns the whole block to the width of its widest line, not each line individually, so shorter lines are not re-centered on their own.
- The `Vec3` overloads project the position through the current camera (an `EasyCam` scope or the default screen) and draw the label as a screen-facing billboard with no depth test, so it is always drawn on top of the 3D scene. On the default screen, `z = 0` lines up exactly with the 2D coordinates. A point behind the camera draws nothing. `screenFixed = true` keeps a constant pixel size regardless of distance; `screenFixed = false` scales the label in world units at its depth, so it shrinks with distance (an extra `scale` multiplies this size in that overload).
- The first draw of a character that has not been used before updates the shared font atlas texture; later draws of the same characters are cheap.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    setColor(1, 1, 1);
    drawBitmapString("FPS: " + to_string(getFrameRate()), 10, 10);
}
```

## drawBitmapStringHighlight

- Draws `text` the same way as `drawBitmapString`, but first fills a solid rectangle behind it so the text stays readable over any background. `background` defaults to black and `foreground` to white; pass your own `Color` values to change either.
- The background rectangle is sized to the text's measured width and height (adding horizontal padding only, so adjacent lines do not overlap) and is positioned using the same alignment currently set by `setTextAlign()`.
- Unlike `drawBitmapString`, this function has no `Vec3`, `screenFixed` or `scale` overload: it always draws in screen-fixed 2D, at (x, y) in the current coordinate space.
- It saves and restores your drawing style internally (equivalent to `pushStyle()`/`popStyle()`), so calling it does not change your current fill/stroke state or color afterward.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    drawBitmapStringHighlight("Paused", 20, 20, Color(0, 0, 0), Color(1, 1, 0));
}
```

## drawBox

- Takes `width`, `height`, `depth`, or a single `size` for a cube. An overload that takes a `Vec3 pos` (or `x, y, z`) first draws the box centered on that point instead of the origin; it is equivalent to `pushMatrix(); translate(pos); drawBox(w, h, d); popMatrix();`.
- The box is always centered on its position: it extends by half of each size in both directions along X, Y and Z.
- Follows the current fill state: it is filled when `fill()` is active, and drawn as a wireframe when `noFill()` is active. See `fill` for the fill/stroke model.
- Uses the current drawing color and respects the matrix stack, so `translate`, `rotate` and `scale` apply as with any other shape. See `pushMatrix` for the matrix stack.
- The screen starts in orthographic projection by default, so a box drawn without perspective shows no foreshortening with distance. Call `setupScreenPerspective()` (or use `EasyCam`) for a perspective view.
- Nearer and farther boxes are not automatically sorted against overlapping shapes unless depth testing is enabled. See `enableDepthTest` for when it is needed and what it affects.

```cpp
void tcApp::setup() {
    setupScreenPerspective();   // enable perspective so the box has depth
    enableDepthTest();
}

void tcApp::draw() {
    drawBox(Vec3(0, 0, 0), 100, 60, 80);   // centered at origin
}
```

## drawCircle

- Draws a circle with center `(cx, cy)` and the given `radius`. A `Vec3 center` version is also available for 3D.
- **The position is the center of the circle**, not a corner as in `drawRect`. Otherwise the coordinates work the same way as in `drawRect`: local coordinates in logical units.
- After `fill()` the circle is filled, and after `noFill()` only its outline is drawn.
- The circle is drawn as a polygon. The number of segments follows the current curve settings, which you can change with `setCurveTolerance` or `setCurveResolution`. In the default Tolerance mode, a larger `radius` or a smaller tolerance uses more segments and costs more to draw.
- To draw only part of a circle, such as a pie slice or an arc, use `drawArc`.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    setColor(1.0f, 0.5f, 0.0f);
    drawCircle(getWidth() / 2, getHeight() / 2, 50);   // position is the center
}
```

## drawCone

- Takes a base `radius`, a `height`, and an optional `resolution` (default 16), the number of segments around the base circle; a higher resolution gives a rounder, more expensive cone. An overload that takes a `Vec3 pos` (or `x, y, z`) first draws the cone centered on that point instead of the origin, equivalent to `pushMatrix(); translate(pos); drawCone(radius, height, resolution); popMatrix();`.
- The cone is centered on its position along the vertical (Y) axis: the apex sits half the height above it and the base circle half the height below it; the base is not pinned to Y = 0.
- Follows the current fill state: it is filled when `fill()` is active, and drawn as a wireframe when `noFill()` is active. See `fill` for the fill/stroke model.
- Uses the current drawing color and respects the matrix stack. See `pushMatrix` for the matrix stack.
- The screen starts in orthographic projection by default, so a cone drawn without perspective shows no foreshortening with distance. Call `setupScreenPerspective()` (or use `EasyCam`) for a perspective view.
- Nearer and farther cones are not automatically sorted against overlapping shapes unless depth testing is enabled. See `enableDepthTest` for when it is needed and what it affects.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    drawCone(Vec3(0, 0, 0), 40, 100);   // apex up, base down, centered at origin
}
```

## drawCurve

- `drawCurve(p0, p1, p2, p3)` draws a smooth Catmull-Rom curve from `p1` to `p2`. The curve passes exactly through `p1` and `p2`. `p0` and `p3` are not on the curve. They only set the direction of the curve at its two ends. This works the same way as `ofDrawCurve` and `curveVertex` in openFrameworks.
- `drawCurve(vector<Vec3>)` draws one smooth curve through a list of points. It needs at least 4 points. The first and last points only set the direction, so the curve runs from the second point to the second-to-last point.
- `drawCurve(points, true)` draws a closed loop that passes through all of the points and returns to the first one. 3 points are enough.

```cpp
vector<Vec3> pts = {Vec3(50,200,0), Vec3(100,50,0),
                     Vec3(250,50,0), Vec3(300,200,0)};
drawCurve(pts);         // open curve
drawCurve(pts, true);   // closed loop through all 4 points
```

- Like `drawBezier`, `drawCurve` always draws a thin 1px line. It ignores `fill()` and `noFill()` and the stroke weight.
- Curves are drawn as many short line segments. The curve settings below decide how many. They are shared by `drawBezier`, `drawCurve`, `appendCurve` and the circle, ellipse, arc and rounded-shape functions. They are part of the current `Style`, and only one of the two modes is active at a time. Setting one mode turns the other off.
- Tolerance mode is the default. TrussC chooses the number of segments so that the line stays within the given distance of the true curve on screen. The current scale is taken into account. Set it with `setCurveTolerance(pixels)`. The default is 0.1 pixels.
- Resolution mode uses a fixed number of segments, regardless of size or zoom. It is useful for an intentionally angular look, or to limit the cost of drawing many small curves. Set it with `setCurveResolution(n)`. The built-in value is 60.

## drawEllipse

- Draws an ellipse with center `(cx, cy)`, horizontal radius `rx` and vertical radius `ry`. A `Vec3 center` version is also available for 3D.
- Like `drawCircle`, **the position is the center**, not a corner. Otherwise the coordinates work the same way as in `drawRect`.
- After `fill()` the ellipse is filled, and after `noFill()` only its outline is drawn.
- `drawCircle(center, r)` gives the same result as `drawEllipse(center, r, r)`.
- The number of segments is decided from the larger of `rx` and `ry`, using the current curve settings. You can change them with `setCurveTolerance` or `setCurveResolution`.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    setColor(0.3f, 0.8f, 0.3f);
    drawEllipse(200, 150, 80, 40);   // rx=80, ry=40, centered at (200, 150)
}
```

## drawLine

- Draws a straight line from `(x1, y1)` to `(x2, y2)`. For 3D, pass two `Vec3` points or six floats. The coordinates work the same way as in `drawRect`: local coordinates in logical units.
- **The line is always 1 pixel wide.** `fill()`, `noFill()` and `setStrokeWeight` have no effect on it.
- For a thick line with a chosen cap and join style, use `drawStroke` instead.
- To draw many separate line segments efficiently at once, use `beginLines()` and `endLines()`.
- Known issue: [#915](https://github.com/TrussC-org/TrussC/issues/915) (the line is always 1 pixel wide; setStrokeWeight() has no effect).

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    setColor(1.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f);
    drawLine(0, 0, getWidth(), getHeight());   // diagonal, 1px fixed width
}
```

## drawPoint

- Draws one point at `(x, y)`. A `Vec3 pos` version is also available for 3D. The coordinates work the same way as in `drawRect`: local coordinates in logical units.
- `fill()` and `noFill()` have no effect, because a point is a single mark.
- The size and the look of the point are not set by `drawPoint` itself. Use `setPointSize` for the size and `setPointStyle` for the look. The look can be a square (`PointStyle::Square`, the default), an anti-aliased round dot (`PointStyle::Round`), or a true 1-pixel point (`PointStyle::Pixel`).

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    setColor(1.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f);
    setPointSize(6);
    setPointStyle(PointStyle::Round);
    drawPoint(200, 150);
}
```

## drawRect

- Draws a rectangle whose top-left corner is at `(x, y)`, with width `w` and height `h`. You can also pass `Vec3 pos, Vec2 size`.
- The origin `(0, 0)` is the top-left corner of the window (or of the current drawing target). `x` grows to the right and `y` grows downward. All 2D shapes in this group use these coordinates.
- Coordinates are in logical units. They are the same numbers as the window size you passed to `setSize`, also on Retina and other high-resolution screens.
- Coordinates are local, so `translate`, `rotate` and `scale` (usually between `pushMatrix` and `popMatrix`) move, turn and resize the rectangle.
- `(x, y)` is always the top-left corner. Unlike `ofRectMode` in openFrameworks, there is no setting to use the center instead. To place a rectangle by its center, subtract half the size yourself: `drawRect(cx - w / 2, cy - h / 2, w, h)`.
- After `fill()` the rectangle is filled with the current color, and after `noFill()` only its outline is drawn. See `fill` for details and defaults.
- `w` and `h` may be negative. The rectangle is then drawn on the other side of `(x, y)`, so you do not need to fix the values yourself.
- With a `Vec3` position, the rectangle is placed at that `z` in a 3D scene.
- For rounded corners, use `drawRectRounded` or `drawRectSquircle`.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    setColor(0.2f, 0.6f, 1.0f);
    fill();
    drawRect(100, 100, 200, 80);   // top-left corner at (100, 100)

    noFill();
    drawRect(100, 220, 200, 80);   // outline only
}
```

## drawRectRounded

- Draws a rectangle with rounded corners. The arguments `(x, y, w, h)` or `Vec3 pos, Vec2 size` and the top-left corner position work the same way as in `drawRect`. `radius` is the radius of the round corners.
- Each corner is a quarter of a circle.
- `radius` is limited to half of the shorter side. A very large value therefore gives a pill (capsule) shape and never distorts the rectangle. A `radius` of `0` or less draws a plain `drawRect`.
- After `fill()` the shape is filled, and after `noFill()` only its outline is drawn.
- Negative `w` and `h` work in the same way as in `drawRect`.
- The number of segments in each corner follows the current curve settings. You can change them with `setCurveTolerance` or `setCurveResolution`.
- The rounded rectangle is always drawn at local `z = 0`, and `pos.z` is ignored. When it falls back to a plain rectangle, `pos.z` is used.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    setColor(1.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f);
    drawRectRounded(100, 100, 200, 80, 16);   // 16px corner radius
}
```

## drawRectSquircle

- Draws a rectangle with smoothly rounded corners. The arguments, the top-left corner position and the limit on `radius` are the same as in `drawRectRounded`. See `drawRect` for how the coordinates work.
- Only the shape of the corners is different. Each corner follows a superellipse curve (`n = 4`) instead of a circular arc. The corner joins the straight edges smoothly, with no visible seam. This is the "squircle" look known from iOS app icons.
- After `fill()` the shape is filled, and after `noFill()` only its outline is drawn.
- The corner calculation is a little more costly than in `drawRectRounded` with the same radius. If the difference does not matter visually, `drawRectRounded` is the better choice.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    setColor(1.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f);
    drawRectSquircle(100, 100, 200, 80, 24);   // iOS-style smooth corners
}
```

## drawSphere

- Takes a `radius` and an optional `resolution` (default 16), the number of rings and sectors used to tessellate the sphere; a higher resolution gives a smoother, more expensive sphere. An overload that takes a `Vec3 pos` (or `x, y, z`) first draws the sphere centered on that point instead of the origin, equivalent to `pushMatrix(); translate(pos); drawSphere(radius, resolution); popMatrix();`.
- The sphere is always centered on its position.
- Follows the current fill state: it is filled when `fill()` is active, and drawn as a wireframe when `noFill()` is active. See `fill` for the fill/stroke model.
- Uses the current drawing color and respects the matrix stack. See `pushMatrix` for the matrix stack.
- The screen starts in orthographic projection by default, so a sphere drawn without perspective shows no foreshortening with distance. Call `setupScreenPerspective()` (or use `EasyCam`) for a perspective view.
- Nearer and farther spheres are not automatically sorted against overlapping shapes unless depth testing is enabled. See `enableDepthTest` for when it is needed and what it affects.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    drawSphere(Vec3(0, 0, 0), 50);        // default resolution (16)
    drawSphere(Vec3(150, 0, 0), 50, 32);  // smoother, more triangles
}
```

## drawStroke

- Draws one thick line between two points. It uses the current `setStrokeWeight` and `setStrokeCap`. You can pass `Vec2` points or `(x1, y1, x2, y2)`.

```cpp
setStrokeWeight(6);
setStrokeCap(StrokeCap::Round);
drawStroke(Vec2(20, 20), Vec2(220, 120));
```

- It is a shorthand for `beginStroke()`, two `vertex()` calls and `endStroke()`. A two-point line has no corner, so `setStrokeJoin` has no visible effect here.
- For a line with several connected segments, use `beginStroke`, `vertex` and `endStroke` directly. Calling `drawStroke` once per segment also works, but each call builds its own small mesh and the corners are not joined.

## drawSuperellipse

- Draws a superellipse (Lamé curve, `|x/rx|^n + |y/ry|^n = 1`) that fits exactly inside the rectangle `(x, y, w, h)`. The arguments `(x, y, w, h)` or `Vec3 pos, Vec2 size` and the top-left corner position work the same way as in `drawRect`.
- The whole outline is one continuous curve. `drawRectSquircle` rounds only the corners and keeps straight edges between them. You can use `drawSuperellipse` in place of `drawRectRounded` when you want one continuous outline.
- The exponent `n` changes the whole shape. `2` gives an ellipse, `4` a squircle, and larger values come closer to the rectangle. `1` gives a diamond, and values below `1` give a star-like shape that curves inward.
- The default `n = 5` is close to the shape of an Apple app icon. The classic Piet Hein superellipse uses `n = 2.5`. Nothing is drawn when `n <= 0`.
- The proportions come from `w` and `h`. A rectangle that is not square gives a stretched shape.
- After `fill()` the shape is filled, and after `noFill()` only its outline is drawn. Shapes with `n` below `1` are also filled correctly, because the fill is built from the center. `appendSuperellipse` does not fill these shapes correctly.

```cpp
void tcApp::draw() {
    setColor(1.0f, 0.4f, 0.7f);
    drawSuperellipse(100, 100, 160, 160);        // n=5, Apple-icon-like
    drawSuperellipse(300, 100, 160, 160, 2.5f);   // Piet Hein's superellipse
}
```
